description: This is Shadow Signals, and we're taking on the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. We're fascinated by the Moon's south pole, a region where the Sun barely rises above the horizon, craters stay in permanent shadow, and Earth can slip out of view. We want to build an intuitive web app where users pick a landing site and a date, then instantly see where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the local horizon.
summary:
This project, titled PENUMBRA, is a slip-proof mission navigator for the lunar south pole. Most tools generally look at “where are the Sun and Earth above this point on this date?” These are important, but don't paint the full picture. However, PENUMBRA answers the question mission teams actually face: if the launch slips or the lander comes down off target, does the mission survive, and what is the best Plan B to follow with? 

It treats a landing as a cloud of possible points and dates, not a single pin. NASA LRO LOLA terrain and JPL SPICE ephemerides drive a horizon engine (9,216 ray-cast points per site), which then feeds into a simulator of solar power, battery charge and Deep Space Network contact. A Monte Carlo over the landing ellipse and LOLA’s height uncertainty gives each site and date a survival probability, that is also mapped out on the cloud. Users can pick any spot, enter their own lander, and test a lunar relay. A Plan B Finder searches nearby points for landing and later dates, and a "Why?" engine names the cause of each change, down to a specific blocking ridge.

The SURVIVOR AI, trained on our own physics runs, screens candidates 3x faster, and anything uncertain is re-checked by exact physics. We also built a second model, HELIOS, but due to it's inaccuracy, it is reported but not used. Results are validated against JPL Horizons, NASA illumination maps, real LRO photos and Chandrayaan-3’s mission timeline to ensure reliable, and cross-referenced data.
details:
The PENUMBRA Project is designed to help out mission planners, educators and the general public, in order to assist them in comparing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates in seconds only. It shows where the Sun and Earth sit against the real terrain horizon, and what that can mean for power, battery life and direct communication with Earth. It brings together several different domains, all with their distinct set of variables (orbital geometry, terrain ray-casting, power systems, Monte Carlo uncertainty, machine learning and independent validation) accounted for by an original Physics Engine.

It is built around the problem that the challenge itself proposes here. Missions rarely keep their dates, and at the south pole a few days or a few hundred meters can decide whether a lander lives. In March 2025, IM-2 Athena came down about 250m from its target near Mons Mouton, inside a shadowed crater. Due to this slight inaccuracy, it could not recharge and went silent within about 13 hours itself. A tool that judges only the target point would have called that site safe.

PENUMBRA has six modules that all run on one physics engine, so that landers can account for every factor when choosing a landing site.

Sky Engine. For any point and minute, it computes the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth, along with the terrain horizon in that direction, and how much of each disc is visible.

  • The Sun’s disc is 0.53° wide, so the engine models partial sunlight instead of treating the Sun as simply “up” or “down”.
  • It includes Earth’s parallax from the site and lunar libration, through the JPL DE440 Moon orientation.
  • With no atmosphere there is no refraction, so the horizon is the terrain itself, on a curved Moon. The engine also reports how much darkness is caused by terrain rather than by the Moon’s curvature alone.
  • The directions of the Sun and the Earth in the Moon-fixed frame are the same for every site, so one hourly table for 2023–2033 directly goes to the browser itself.
  • Each of the 9,216 analysed points per site across five south-pole sites, including three of NASA’s nine Artemis III candidate regions (Malapert, Haworth, Nobile Rim 2 has its own 360-bin horizon mask, ray-cast 200 km out over NASA LOLA 5m terrain with an 80m far field. Every query is also a lookup and a rotation, so a full 14-day mission is simulated in the browser in milliseconds only.

Mission Board. Five site-and-date cards side by side: the planned date, the slipped date, and the other sites on the slipped date.

  • Each card shows time to sunset and Earthset (or to sunrise, if landing in darkness), % of time sunlit, % with Earth in view, % with both, % with a direct-to-Earth link, the longest night and the longest comms blackout. It gives a survive/fail verdict with hours until the battery floor, plus the local landing slope.
  • A slip slider spans every landing day of 2027 and re-plans every card at once. Its track is colored by whether a 14-day mission survives a landing on each day, and the longest survivable windows are just a click away.
  • A clickable map lets the user pick any of the 9,216 points per site, coloured by sunlight, Earth visibility or slope. The whole 2027 survival track for that exact spot is recomputed live in about a second in the software due to it's native AI systems.
  • Below the cards there are engineering readouts with the smallest battery that survives (sequent-peak sizing); a 360° horizon panorama; and a 14-day timeline of sunlight, Earth, DSN visibility and battery charge.

Survival Simulator. This module models the lander itself alongside the lunar sky.

  • Power & Battery: It supports four panel layouts (four vertical faces, a Sun-tracking mast, a horizontal deck, and a lander tipped on its side) at a 2 m panel height, accounting for partial-disc sunlight. From there, it tracks the battery’s state of charge in 10-minute steps, factoring in operational loads, a survival heater, and a hard floor below which the mission is lost.
  • Communications & Relays: To establish a direct link, Earth has to sit at least 1° above the real terrain while at least one Deep Space Network complex (Goldstone, Madrid, or Canberra) has line-of-sight to the Moon. We also built in a "what-if" toggle for one or two relays in an elliptical lunar frozen orbit—modeled on NASA’s LCRNS reference orbit and ESA’s Lunar Pathfinder, and clearly labeled as an assumption. For a 14 February 2027 landing, adding just one relay drops the longest blackout from 198 h down to 4.8 h at Shackleton, from 174 h to 4.5 h at Malapert, and from 167 h to 4.5 h at Leibnitz beta.
  • Custom Landers: Users can test three generic lander presets or input their own hardware specs (battery capacity, panel area and layout, cell efficiency, load, heater, and battery floor). Every card, track, and search updates live on the dashboard, and all presets are strictly labeled as generic rather than real spacecraft.

Dispersion Cloud. Because landers rarely hit a pinpoint target, PENUMBRA samples 4,000 touchdown points across a 400 m (3σ) landing ellipse, running each one across 10 terrain-height variants built from the LOLA height-error maps in PGDA 78. This generates a survival heatmap that flags lethal shadow pockets, calculates an overall probability of survival, and suggests a safer aim point. Our runs show that simply aiming at the best-lit pixel isn't enough: P(survive) across the full ellipse is only 11.6% at Shackleton (despite being 80% at the center aim cell), 45.3% at Malapert, and 31.3% at Leibnitz beta (100% at the aim cell). Shifting the aim point just 263–388 m away roughly doubles those survival odds. We also report the IM-2 replay honestly: none of the 27 NASA 5 m maps we checked cover the landing site, and on 80 m terrain, the crater Athena came to rest in is smaller than a single pixel—a data-resolution limit we make sure to disclose on screen.

Plan B Finder and "Why?" Engine.

  • Plan B: When a launch slips, this tool searches every point within 2 km with a slope under 8°, checking every subsequent date up to 30 days out (since you can't land before the slipped date). It ranks surviving options first, sorting by the smallest delay, shortest comms blackout, and most sunlight. For example, Option A finds physics-verified solutions at Shackleton (162 m away, +6 days), Malapert (1.1 km away, +18 days), and Leibnitz beta (535 m away, +17 days).
  • Why? Engine: To explain why a site fails or succeeds, this engine compares two scenarios by isolating one variable at a time: the Sun’s path (season and date), Earth’s path (libration) and DSN windows, the terrain horizon, or panel height. It attributes the exact percentage change to each factor and identifies the specific blocking ridge by its azimuth, distance, and height. At Malapert, for instance, delaying a landing by 12 days drops sunlight from 100% to 54.6%—which is entirely due to the Sun’s path, whereas the local terrain alone would have cut it to 13%.

Two Lenses on One Engine.

  • Planner View: Built for science and engineering teams, offering dense telemetry readouts, CSV and JSON exports, and shareable URLs that encode the entire scenario (site, point, lander, and date) so everyone is looking at the exact same numbers.
  • Public View: Designed for outreach and accessibility, featuring a first-person "stand on the rim" view of the real horizon, a side-by-side comparison with the Sun’s elevation over your own city, and a sonified lunar day for blind and low-vision users where audio pitch tracks the Sun's height and silence marks the lunar night.

The AI Layer. We trained two machine learning models on labels generated directly by our physics engine—giving us plentiful, exact training data with zero manual labeling. Both models had to pass strict pre-set acceptance gates before being trusted in the app:

  • HELIOS (Neural Horizon Field): Inspired by DLR’s Fourier-compressed horizon maps, this model uses Gaussian Fourier features feeding a 4-layer neural network to output 127 Fourier coefficients of the 360° horizon as a continuous field. We weighted the training loss five times more heavily between −2° and +8°—the critical band where the Sun and Earth sit and where a tenth of a degree decides whether a solar panel is lit. On held-out terrain tiles, however, its median error was 0.23–0.83° against our strict 0.05° gate. Because it failed our accuracy rules, we report it transparently in the project but do not use it, relying on exact ray-traced horizons instead.
  • SURVIVOR: This ensemble of gradient-boosted models (LightGBM) was trained on 75,000 exact simulator runs to read Sun/Earth geometry, horizon features, and lander settings, predicting survival probability, energy, longest blackout, and time to the battery floor. Its probabilities are calibrated via isotonic regression, bounded by split-conformal intervals, and guarded by a nearest-neighbor detector that flags out-of-distribution inputs. An AI prediction is only accepted if its confidence interval sits cleanly on one side of the survival threshold and the input is in-distribution. All top picks and borderline cases are re-run in the exact simulator, and every number on screen is clearly tagged as either "physics-verified" or "AI, within bounds."
  • AI Performance: On Leibnitz beta—a site held out completely from training—SURVIVOR achieved an AUROC of 0.9975 with a calibration error of 0.005, reaching 99.81% accuracy on the 81% of runs it accepts alone. Because interval coverage was 78–96% against a 90 ± 2% gate, we strictly use it as a fast screener rather than a final verdict. Across a search of 276,480 candidates per site, only 1.3%, 1.9%, and 27% needed to be passed to the exact simulator, delivering a 3.1× end-to-end speed-up. All 20 of the AI's top picks survived exact verification at every site (though exact physics swapped the #1 pick at 2 of the 3 sites), and because 7 to 8 of the AI's top 10 raw picks sat on slopes steeper than 8°, the slope-filtered Plan B engine—not the raw AI—always makes the final landing recommendation.

How It Was Validated. Our built-in Trust tab lays out our independent verification checks alongside our honest limitations:

  • Ephemeris Accuracy: Across 726 site–time comparisons against NASA/JPL Horizons at three south-pole sites, our Sun and Earth directions had a maximum error of just 0.000027°.
  • Long-Term Illumination: Compared against NASA’s PGDA 69 LOLA polar illumination maps over 18.6 years (300 points), our model achieved R2=0.859R^2 = 0.859R2=0.859 (r=0.947r = 0.947r=0.947, with a −2.9 percentage point bias).
  • Real Imagery Overlay: Overlaying our predicted shadows onto an actual LRO camera image taken at a known timestamp (LROC NAC M128378248LC) yielded an overlap (IoU) of 0.71, with 95.2% agreement across 233,000 cells.
  • Mission Timeline Check: At Chandrayaan-3’s landing site (69.373°S, 32.319°E), our engine predicts sunset on 4 September 2023 and sunrise on 19–20 September—matching ISRO’s public timeline, which put the lander and rover to sleep in early September and anticipated sunrise around 22 September.
  • Engine Parity & Limits: Our browser-based TypeScript simulator matches the offline Python pipeline with identical survival verdicts across 365 of 365 landing days and 108 of 108 audited board states. While LOLA terrain-height uncertainties are propagated into our dispersion results, we explicitly state on screen what PENUMBRA does not claim: mission-grade certification, exact wattage for real spacecraft, or thermal survival modeling.

Data Sources. Every result in the app cites the exact dataset used to generate it:

  • NASA (Primary): LRO LOLA topography (PGDA 78 5 m site maps and height-error maps for Shackleton, Malapert, Leibnitz beta, Haworth, and Nobile Rim 2; plus the PGDA 90 80 m polar map), PGDA 69 polar illumination products, JPL NAIF SPICE (DE440 ephemeris and Moon orientation for libration), JPL Horizons, LROC NAC imagery, DSN complex coordinates, and the LCRNS relay reference orbit.
  • Partner Agencies (Cross-checks & Optional Layers): ISRO (Chandrayaan-3 landing site and timeline for validation), ESA (Lunar Pathfinder and Moonlight relay concepts for the relay what-if), and CNSA (Chang’e-7’s planned Shackleton-rim landing for site context).

Tools and Languages.

  • Offline Pipeline & ML: Built in Python using SpiceyPy, NumPy, SciPy, Numba (for parallel ray-casting), and rasterio, with LightGBM and scikit-learn powering SURVIVOR and PyTorch used to train HELIOS.
  • Web App & Hosting: Built with TypeScript, React, and Vite, featuring custom SVG and canvas charts, Web Audio for sonification, and a full TypeScript port of the simulator running natively in the browser. It is hosted as a static site on GitHub Pages (https://darsh123456789.github.io/Penumbra/) using compact binary data files so nothing relies on an external server during judging, with all code open-sourced athttps://github.com/Darsh123456789/penumbra.

Benefits and Intended Impact. PENUMBRA turns a multi-tool, multi-hour engineering analysis into a few seconds of interactive exploration, giving mission planners a direct answer to launch slips alongside ranked, explained alternatives and shareable scenario links. More importantly, by treating landing dispersion as a core part of site selection rather than an afterthought, it exposes the exact shadow-pocket failure mode behind recent south-pole losses before launch rather than after touchdown. Our analysis shows that landing date actually matters more than battery size: even at the best-lit points, only 55–58% of 2027 landing days are survivable due to lunar nights lasting 66–154 hours. This directly supports upcoming missions on the manifest, including CLPS deliveries like Griffin-1, Chang’e-7’s move to 2027, and NASA’s candidate regions for Artemis IV.

Why It Is Creative & What We Considered. Rather than treating a landing as a single pin on a map, PENUMBRA treats it as a probability cloud and directly answers "will this hardware survive here on this date?" instead of leaving engineers to interpret raw elevation angles on their own. Its counterfactual explanations point to the exact ridge responsible for a failure that a single-point check would have cleared, and its AI layer is held to strict statistical guarantees with an exact physics fallback—even openly documenting the model that failed its gates. Throughout development, we balanced physical accuracy (real topography, zero atmospheric refraction, lunar curvature, Earth libration and parallax, finite solar disc, observer height, terrain-error propagation, and landing slope) with browser-level speed via offline precomputation, accessibility (text labels alongside colors, keyboard navigation, audio sonification, and mobile responsiveness), and complete openness through public data and open-source code.
